title: Why are hamate bone injuries popping up with so many MLB stars?
content:
Before MLB spring training even began this month, hamate bone injuries claimed some of baseball’s biggest names.

Arizona Diamondbacks outfielder Corbin Carroll, New York Mets shortstop Francisco Lindor and Baltimore Orioles second baseman Jackson Holliday have recently fallen victim to the bone injury, calling their Opening Day availability into question.

Carroll will miss playing for the United States in the World Baseball Classic because of it. Lindor had surgery Feb. 11 and is going through what will be a minimum six-week recovery.

The hamate bone is a small, hook-shaped bone in the outer wrist. Its function is to help connect the wrist to the hand. It is also essential for the ring and pinky fingers, which contribute to power gripping, and it aids in the movement and flexibility of the wrist and fingers.

When batters grip a bat, the knob often presses against the hamate bone. The bone can withstand intermittent pressure with little harm. But for hitters who swing a bat thousands of times, the bone starts to weaken from constant pressure, and that can eventually lead to stress fractures.

Although anyone can injure a hamate bone falling on a hand, a hamate injury is most common in athletes, according to Dr. Joseph Styron, a hand surgeon for the Cleveland Clinic.

“It just tends to be more common in athletes because of the nature of holding objects in their hand,” Styron said. “In the baseball bat, in particular, I see it most commonly.”

Once the bone has experienced enough wear and tear, any sudden increase in pressure, like a hard line drive or foul tip, can cause a fracture. Even without a batter hitting the ball, the pressure generated by simply checking a swing can also damage the bone. Checked swings are considered one of the more common causes.

Hamate bone injuries are also common with hockey players, golfers or anyone who has to swing an object into hard stops, according to Styron.

Surgeons often opt to “excise” (medical terminology for remove) the bone altogether in surgery, similar to an appendix. There isn’t sufficient blood flow to the bone to facilitate enough healing, and athletes can return to full strength without it.

“Our attempts to fix them in the past haven’t always worked out very well,” Styron said. “So we’ve found that just excising it, people do very well functionally without it.”

This generally removes the likelihood of reinjury. With modern strength conditioning programs in professional sports, the risk of removal affecting a player’s performance is traditionally low.

The standard recovery after surgery is typically six to eight weeks. The recovery time isn’t even from losing the bone, but more for the scar tissue to heal and the pain of placing a bat on it to subside.
